Potato remains well below last year’s level despite a gradual recovery, while tomato prices ease from early-September highs, underscoring sharply different supply-demand dynamics across key perishables

Wholesale onion prices have emerged as the biggest pressure point in India’s key vegetable basket, with the average mandi price rising to Rs 3,736.61 per quintal on September 15, 2026, compared with Rs 946.60 a year earlier. That represents an increase of nearly 295 per cent, highlighting a dramatic reversal from the relatively subdued price environment seen in September 2025. The onion market has also witnessed a sharp repricing within the current month. Prices climbed from Rs 2,422.80 per quintal on August 15 to Rs 3,656.71 by August 25, before moving to Rs 3,539.67 on September 1 and then recovering to Rs 3,702.51 on September 8. By September 15, prices had edged up further to Rs 3,736.61. The latest level is around 54 per cent above the August 15 price, although the pace of increase has moderated considerably after the sharp jump seen in the second half of August.

The year-on-year comparison makes the onion movement particularly stark. On September 15, 2024, the mandi price stood at Rs 3,924.18 per quintal, meaning the current price is still slightly below the level recorded two years ago. But compared with the unusually low Rs 946.60 recorded on September 15, 2025, the market has undergone a near fourfold recovery. The data therefore points to a significant base effect alongside a genuine tightening or repricing of the market relative to last year. Potatoes, by contrast, remain in a substantially softer price regime. The wholesale price was Rs 789.80 per quintal on September 15, up from Rs 716.57 on August 15 and Rs 723.80 on August 25. Prices have consequently risen by about 10 per cent over the month and 9 per cent since August 25, indicating a gradual firming rather than a sudden price shock. Yet the year-on-year picture remains weak: the September 15, 2026 price is about 26 per cent below Rs 1,071.91 recorded on the same day in 2025 and nearly 63 per cent below the Rs 2,128.36 recorded in September 2024.

Tomatoes occupy a middle ground. Their wholesale price declined from Rs 1,784.91 per quintal on August 15 to Rs 1,646.12 on August 25, before climbing to Rs 1,914.86 on September 1. Prices subsequently moderated to Rs 1,868.55 on September 8 and Rs 1,692.44 on September 15. The latest price is therefore about 5 per cent lower than the August 15 level and nearly 12 per cent below the September 1 peak, suggesting that the early-September firmness has begun to unwind. Even so, tomato prices remain higher than a year earlier. The September 15, 2026 level of Rs 1,692.44 per quintal is about 21 per cent above Rs 1,402.67 recorded on September 15, 2025, although it remains substantially below the Rs 2,333.05 seen in September 2024.

Taken together, the three commodities show that the vegetable market is not moving in a single direction. Onion has undergone a pronounced year-on-year price escalation, potato remains structurally cheaper than a year ago despite a recent recovery, and tomato is oscillating within a relatively narrower range. The divergence matters because movements in the headline vegetable basket can mask very different supply and price conditions at the commodity level. The latest numbers also suggest that momentum rather than simply the absolute price level will be important to watch in the coming weeks. Onion prices have continued to rise after the sharp August repricing, potato has been steadily recovering from a low base, while tomato has already retreated from its early-September high. For consumers, traders and policymakers, the trajectory of these individual markets could therefore prove more informative than a single aggregate vegetable-price signal.
